title: Japan Sends a Spacecraft to Collect Pieces of a Mars Moon
summary:
Japan's space agency, JAXA, planned to launch a special mission to Phobos, one of the two moons of Mars, on Monday, and anyone could watch it live online.

The mission is called MMX, which stands for Martian Moons eXploration. Its goal is to collect samples from Phobos, the larger of Mars' two moons, and bring them back to Earth so scientists can study them. If the mission succeeds, the samples could help solve a long-standing mystery: how the moons of Mars formed.

An American astronomer named Asaph Hall discovered Phobos and its smaller sibling, Deimos, in 1877. Their names are pretty dramatic. Phobos comes from an ancient Greek word meaning "fear," and Deimos comes from a Greek word meaning "dread."

Even though scientists have paid a lot of attention to Mars, they still do not know exactly where its moons came from. One idea is that they were once asteroids. Another is that they formed from leftover material from the early days of the solar system, about 4.5 billion years ago.

Although MMX is a Japanese mission, NASA helped by providing instruments and technology. Nicky Fox, a NASA science leader, said the samples "will bring forth paradigm-shifting science on the Mars system for generations to come," especially as NASA prepares to send the first humans to Mars.

The spacecraft was set to launch on an H3 rocket from Japan's Tanegashima Space Center at 3:41 p.m. Eastern time on Monday, October 19. That was 4:41 a.m. on October 20 in Japan. The launch could be watched on JAXA's YouTube page.

The trip is a long one. MMX is expected to reach Phobos in August 2027 and study its surface for at least 16 months before collecting samples. The samples will not come back to Earth until at least 2031.
why_it_matters: Bringing back real pieces of a Mars moon could solve a long-standing mystery about how the moons formed and help prepare for future human trips to Mars.

background_read: Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, which are much smaller and more oddly shaped than Earth's Moon.
A sample-return mission sends a spacecraft to collect material from another world and carry it back so scientists can study it with powerful lab tools on Earth.
Space agencies often work together, sharing instruments and technology so that one mission can do more science.
Because space is so vast, trips to Mars and back take years, so scientists plan these missions far ahead.
